client: Hey Luna, I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately. My thesis deadlines are creeping up, and I'm also trying to manage my part-time job and keep up with social commitments. It's just a lot, and I'm not sure how to handle it all.
therapist: It sounds like you're under a lot of pressure right now, and it's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed with everything on your plate. What are some of the thoughts that come up for you when you think about managing all these responsibilities?

client: I keep thinking that no matter how hard I try, I won't be able to meet all the deadlines and expectations. It feels like everything is just piling up, and I’m starting to doubt whether I can do it all without messing up.
therapist: It’s really tough when those doubts start to creep in, and it’s natural to feel that way when you have so much on your plate. Let’s break it down a bit—what’s one small step you could take today that might help you feel a little more in control or reduce that overwhelming feeling?

client: I appreciate that, Luna. I guess I could make a to-do list and prioritize what needs to be done first. But I worry that even making the list will just stress me out more because I’ll see everything I have to do.
therapist: It’s totally understandable to feel that way about making a to-do list. Sometimes seeing everything laid out can feel overwhelming. How about starting with a shorter list of just the top three most important tasks for today? That might help you focus on what’s most urgent without feeling as overwhelmed. What do you think about trying that?

client: I see what you mean, Luna. Focusing on just three tasks does sound a bit more manageable. But I’m still a little anxious about how I’ll stick to it and not get distracted by everything else that needs to be done. It’s hard to stay focused when there’s so much going on.
therapist: It’s great that you’re open to trying the three-task approach, and it’s completely normal to feel anxious about staying focused. One strategy could be to set specific times for each task and give yourself short breaks in between to help maintain your concentration. What do you think about setting some specific times for your tasks today?

client: I like the idea of setting specific times for each task. It might help me stay on track. But I’m a bit worried about sticking to the schedule, especially when unexpected things come up. It feels like my day can get derailed so easily.
therapist: It’s really good that you’re thinking through how to manage your schedule, and it’s completely valid to worry about how unexpected things might disrupt your plans. One way to build some flexibility into your schedule is to set aside a buffer time for unexpected tasks or breaks. How about adding a 15-30 minute buffer after each task to help absorb any interruptions? How does that sound?

client: I think adding buffer time could help, Luna. It’s a good idea to have some flexibility. But I’m still a bit skeptical about whether I can actually stick to it. I tend to get sidetracked easily, and sometimes I just end up feeling guilty for taking breaks.
therapist: It’s completely understandable to feel skeptical, and it’s great that you’re being honest about your concerns. Guilt about taking breaks is common, but it’s important to remember that breaks are actually beneficial for productivity and mental well-being. What if you set a specific time for your breaks and treat them as an essential part of your schedule? How do you think that might help with staying on track and reducing guilt?

client: I can see how treating breaks as part of the schedule could help, Luna. But I still worry that I’ll feel guilty for taking time off, and that might make it hard to actually relax during those breaks. It’s a struggle to balance feeling productive and taking care of myself.
therapist: It’s really insightful of you to recognize that guilt can interfere with your ability to relax. Balancing productivity and self-care is definitely a challenge, but it’s important to remember that taking breaks is not a luxury—it’s a necessity for maintaining your well-being and effectiveness. What if you started by setting a small, manageable goal for your breaks, like taking a 10-minute walk or doing a short mindfulness exercise? How do you think that might help you start to see breaks as a positive part of your day?

client: I think starting with a small goal like a 10-minute walk or a mindfulness exercise could be a good way to ease into taking breaks. It feels more doable, but I’m still a bit skeptical about whether I can actually stick to it and not feel guilty. I guess I’ll have to give it a try and see how it goes.
therapist: It’s great that you’re open to giving it a try, even with some skepticism. Starting small can often make it easier to build new habits, and it’s a positive step toward finding a balance that works for you. How about setting a specific time for your first short break today, and perhaps reflecting on how you feel afterward? What do you think about that?

client: I think setting a specific time for my first short break today could be helpful. I’ll try to take a 10-minute walk after I finish my next task. I’m still a bit nervous about how it will go, but I’m willing to give it a shot and see if it helps me feel less overwhelmed.
therapist: That’s a fantastic plan, and I’m really proud of you for taking this step. Trying a 10-minute walk after your next task is a great way to start. It’s normal to feel a bit nervous, but giving it a shot is a brave and positive move. How about taking a moment to visualize how you might feel after the walk? What do you think might be different about your mindset or energy level?

client: I appreciate your encouragement, Luna. When I think about how I might feel after the walk, I imagine I could feel a bit more relaxed and refreshed. Maybe I’ll have a clearer mind and be able to focus better on my next task. It’s a hopeful thought, but I’m still a bit nervous about whether it will actually make a difference.
therapist: It’s wonderful that you’re allowing yourself to imagine feeling more relaxed and refreshed after the walk. That’s a hopeful and positive mindset to have. It’s okay to still feel a bit nervous—that’s a natural part of trying something new. How about taking a few deep breaths right now and setting an intention for your walk, like focusing on the present moment or enjoying the fresh air? How do you think that might help you transition into your break?
